::: lead
I build and evaluate language-based tools for mental health assessment, asking when they work, for whom, and why.
:::

I am a third-year PhD student in the [Department of Psychology](https://psychology.princeton.edu/) at Princeton University, advised by [Erik Nook in the Logic of Emotion Lab](https://lemolab.princeton.edu/). My research sits at the intersection of computer science, natural language processing, and clinical psychology, with a focus on the psychometric validity and generalizability of language-based measures.

My current work examines whether large language models predict depression and anxiety equivalently across racially and ethnically diverse samples, how the semantic content of first-person pronoun use in psychotherapy transcripts tracks symptom severity and treatment response, and whether domain-adapted clinical language models can reliably predict treatment outcomes.

Before Princeton, I was a Lab Manager in Emily Falk's [Communication Neuroscience Lab](https://www.asc.upenn.edu/research/centers/communication-neuroscience-lab) at the University of Pennsylvania. I have also had the privilege of collaborating with Jamie Pennebaker and researchers affiliated with the [World Well-Being Project](https://wwbp.org/).

My research has been supported by the Princeton [Data Driven Social Science Graduate Fellowship](https://ddss.princeton.edu/), the New Jersey Health Foundation, and [Princeton Precision Health](https://pph.princeton.edu/about).

## Research Interests

::: interest-list
-   Development of language-based clinical assessments
-   Language as a transdiagnostic index of psychological distress
-   Domain adaptation and evaluation of large language models for mental health
-   Computational psycholinguistics and large-scale text analysis
:::
